stem.en: Which of these is a vector quantity?

explanation.en: Displacement has both magnitude and direction. Work, speed and temperature are scalars.

stem.en: Two forces of 3 N and 4 N act on a body. Which of these CANNOT be their resultant?

explanation.en: The resultant lies between |4 − 3| = 1 N and 4 + 3 = 7 N, so 8 N is impossible.

solution.en: The resultant lies between |4 − 3| = 1 N and 4 + 3 = 7 N, so 8 N is impossible.

stem.en: Two vectors A and B are equal. This means they have:

options.en: the same magnitude and the same direction

explanation.en: Equal vectors must have equal magnitudes and the same direction; their starting points may differ.

stem.en: Two vectors, each of magnitude P, are added. If the resultant also has magnitude P, the angle between them is:

explanation.en: R² = P² + P² + 2P² cos θ = P² gives cos θ = −1/2, so θ = 120°.

stem.en: A vector of magnitude 10 units makes 30° with the x-axis. Its x-component is:
The magnitude of the vector 6î − 8ĵ is:
The resultant of two vectors of fixed magnitudes is greatest when the angle between them is:

explanation.en: R² = A² + B² + 2AB cos θ is largest when cos θ = 1, i.e. θ = 0°.

stem.en: Two forces of 10 N each act at 120° to each other. Their resultant is:
If A = 2î + 3ĵ and B = î − 4ĵ, the unit vector along A + B is:

explanation.en: A + B = 3î − ĵ, with magnitude √(9 + 1) = √10. The unit vector is (3î − ĵ)/√10.

stem.en: The position of a particle is r = 2t î + 3t² ĵ (in m). Its velocity at t = 1 s is:

explanation.en: v = dr/dt = 2î + 6t ĵ = 2î + 6ĵ m/s at t = 1 s.

stem.en: For the particle with r = 2t î + 3t² ĵ (in m), the acceleration is:

explanation.en: a = dv/dt = d(2î + 6tĵ)/dt = 6ĵ m/s², constant.

stem.en: The velocity of a particle moving along a curved path is always:

options.en: along the tangent to the path

explanation.en: v = dr/dt is the limit of a small displacement along the path, so it is tangent to the path.

stem.en: A particle starts from rest at the origin with acceleration (3î + 4ĵ) m/s². Its speed after 2 s is:

explanation.en: v = at = 6î + 8ĵ m/s, so speed = √(36 + 64) = 10 m/s.

solution.en: v = at = 6î + 8ĵ m/s, so speed = √(36 + 64) = 10 m/s.

stem.en: A particle moves with x = 3t² and y = 4t² (in m). Its path and the magnitude of its acceleration are:

explanation.en: y/x = 4/3 at all times, so the path is the straight line y = 4x/3. aₓ = 6, aᵧ = 8, so |a| = 10 m/s².

stem.en: At the highest point of a projectile's path, which of these is zero?

explanation.en: At the top the vertical velocity is zero; the horizontal velocity u cos θ and the acceleration g remain.

stem.en: For the greatest horizontal range, a projectile should be launched at:

explanation.en: R = u² sin 2θ/g is greatest when sin 2θ = 1, i.e. θ = 45°.

stem.en: A projectile launched at 30° has the same range as one launched with the same speed at:

explanation.en: Complementary angles θ and 90° − θ give the same range: 30° and 60°.

stem.en: A ball is thrown at 20 m/s at 45° to the horizontal. Its horizontal range is (g = 10 m/s²):
The horizontal range of a projectile is 4√3 times its maximum height. The angle of projection is:

explanation.en: R/H = 4/tan θ = 4√3 gives tan θ = 1/√3, so θ = 30°.

stem.en: A stone is thrown horizontally at 10 m/s from a tower 20 m high. It lands at a horizontal distance of (g = 10 m/s²):
In uniform circular motion, which of these remains constant?

explanation.en: Only the magnitude of the velocity (speed) is constant; the direction of velocity and acceleration keeps changing.

stem.en: The direction of the centripetal acceleration is:

explanation.en: Centripetal means centre-seeking: the acceleration points towards the centre of the circle.

stem.en: A body moves in a circle of radius 2 m at a constant speed of 4 m/s. Its centripetal acceleration is:
If the speed of a body in uniform circular motion is doubled on the same circle, its centripetal acceleration becomes:

explanation.en: a = v²/R, so doubling v makes a four times.

solution.en: a = v²/R, so doubling v makes a four times.

stem.en: A wheel makes 300 revolutions per minute. Its angular speed is:

explanation.en: 300 rpm = 5 rev/s, so ω = 2π × 5 = 10π rad/s ≈ 31.4 rad/s.

stem.en:
Assertion (A): For a given speed of projection, the horizontal range of a projectile is the same for angles of projection of 30° and 60°.
Reason (R): The horizontal range of a projectile is maximum when the angle of projection is 45°.

options.en: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

explanation.en: R = u² sin 2θ / g and sin 60° = sin 120°, so the ranges for 30° and 60° are equal. R is also true, but it is the equality sin 2θ = sin (180° − 2θ), not the 45° maximum, that explains A.

stem.en:
Assertion (A): A body in uniform circular motion moves with constant velocity.
Reason (R): In uniform circular motion, the acceleration is always directed towards the centre of the circle.

options.en: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

explanation.en: The speed is constant but the direction of velocity changes continuously, so the velocity is not constant: A is false. The centripetal acceleration points to the centre: R is true.

stem.en: How long is the ball in the air?

passage.en: In a school cricket match, a batter hits the ball from ground level at a speed of 20 m/s at an angle of 30° above the horizontal. A fielder at deep point watches the ball and runs to where he expects it to land. Ignore air resistance and take g = 10 m/s².

stem.en: How far from the batter does the ball land?

passage.en: In a school cricket match, a batter hits the ball from ground level at a speed of 20 m/s at an angle of 30° above the horizontal. A fielder at deep point watches the ball and runs to where he expects it to land. Ignore air resistance and take g = 10 m/s².

stem.en: One or more options may be correct. A projectile is launched from level ground with speed u at an angle θ (0 < θ < 90°). Neglect air resistance. Which statements are correct?

options.en: At the highest point its speed is u cos θ
Launch angles θ and 90° − θ give equal ranges
At the highest point its acceleration is zero
The ratio of maximum height to range is tan θ / 4

explanation.en: At the top vᵧ = 0, so the speed is the horizontal part u cos θ. R = u² sin 2θ/g is the same for θ and 90° − θ. The acceleration is g downward everywhere, never zero. H/R = (u² sin²θ/2g)/(2u² sin θ cos θ/g) = tan θ/4.

stem.en: One or more options may be correct. Two non-zero vectors A and B satisfy |A + B| = |A − B|. Which statements must be true?

explanation.en: |A + B|² − |A − B|² = 4A·B = 0, so A·B = 0 and the vectors are perpendicular; then |A + B|² = A² + B². Nothing forces their magnitudes to be equal.

stem.en: The horizontal range of a projectile on level ground is 4√3 times its maximum height. Find the angle of projection in degrees (integer).

explanation.en: H/R = tan θ/4 = 1/(4√3), so tan θ = 1/√3 and θ = 30°.

stem.en: A particle moves in a circle of radius 0.5 m at a constant 120 revolutions per minute. Find the magnitude of its centripetal acceleration in m/s², correct to two decimal places (take π = 3.1416).
Two forces of 3 N and 4 N act on a body with an angle of 60° between them. The magnitude of their resultant is about
A particle starts from the origin at t = 0 with velocity 3ĵ m/s and moves with constant acceleration 2î m/s². Its position vector at t = 2 s is
The greatest horizontal range a ball can be thrown with a certain speed is 100 m. With the same speed, the greatest height it can reach when thrown vertically up is

explanation.en: R_max = u²/g = 100 m. Thrown straight up, H = u²/2g = 50 m.

stem.en: Which of the following is a vector quantity?

explanation.en: Displacement has both magnitude and direction and adds by the triangle law. Work and pressure are scalars. Electric current has a direction but does not obey vector addition (currents meeting at a junction simply add), so it is treated as a scalar.

stem.en: Two forces of 3 N and 4 N act on a body at right angles to each other. The magnitude of their resultant is:

explanation.en: $R = \sqrt{A^2 + B^2 + 2AB\cos90^\circ} = \sqrt{9 + 16} = 5$ N. 7 N would need the forces parallel and 1 N antiparallel.

stem.en: Two forces of 5 N and 8 N act at a point. Which of the following CANNOT be the magnitude of their resultant?

explanation.en: The resultant lies between $|A - B| = 3$ N (antiparallel) and $A + B = 13$ N (parallel), both included. 2 N is below the minimum, so it is impossible.

stem.en: On level ground, with air resistance neglected, a projectile launched with a given speed has the maximum horizontal range when the angle of projection is:

explanation.en: $R = \dfrac{u^2\sin2\theta}{g}$ is greatest when $\sin2\theta = 1$, i.e. $\theta = 45^\circ$; then $R_{\max} = u^2/g$. At $90^\circ$ the range is zero.

stem.en: A ball projected at $30^\circ$ to the horizontal has a certain range. With the same speed, the same range is obtained at a projection angle of:

explanation.en: $\sin2\theta = \sin(180^\circ - 2\theta)$, so the angles $\theta$ and $90^\circ - \theta$ give the same range. $90^\circ - 30^\circ = 60^\circ$. ($120^\circ$ is a backward throw.)

stem.en: At the highest point of the path of a projectile (no air resistance), which of these is zero?

explanation.en: At the top the vertical velocity $u\sin\theta - gt$ becomes zero, but the horizontal component $u\cos\theta$ remains, so the speed is $u\cos\theta$, not zero. The acceleration is $g$ downward throughout.

options.en: The vertical component of its velocity
The horizontal component of its velocity

stem.en: A car goes round a circular track of radius 5 m at a constant speed of 10 m s$^{-1}$. The magnitude of its acceleration is:

explanation.en: Constant speed in a circle still means changing velocity. The centripetal acceleration is $a_c = \dfrac{v^2}{r} = \dfrac{100}{5} = 20$ m s$^{-2}$, directed toward the centre.

stem.en: Find the magnitude of the vector $2\hat i - 3\hat j + 6\hat k$.

explanation.en: $|\vec A| = \sqrt{2^2 + (-3)^2 + 6^2} = \sqrt{4 + 9 + 36} = \sqrt{49} = 7$. The negative sign of a component does not matter once squared.

stem.en: A stone is thrown horizontally at 10 m s$^{-1}$ from the top of a 20 m high cliff. How far from the foot of the cliff does it land? ($g = 10$ m s$^{-2}$)

explanation.en: Vertical motion starts from zero vertical velocity: $20 = 5t^2 \Rightarrow t = 2$ s. Horizontal motion is uniform: $x = 10\times2 = 20$ m. The horizontal speed does not change the time of fall.

stem.en: Rain falls vertically at 3 m s$^{-1}$. A man walks on a level road at 4 m s$^{-1}$. The speed of the rain relative to the man is:

explanation.en: $\vec v_{rm} = \vec v_r - \vec v_m$. The two are perpendicular, so $|\vec v_{rm}| = \sqrt{3^2 + 4^2} = 5$ m s$^{-1}$; to the man the rain appears to come from in front, slanting toward him.

stem.en: The angular speed of the seconds hand of a clock is:

explanation.en: It turns $2\pi$ rad in 60 s: $\omega = \dfrac{2\pi}{60} = \dfrac{\pi}{30} \approx 0.105$ rad s$^{-1}$. $\pi/1800$ rad s$^{-1}$ belongs to the minute hand.

stem.en:
Assertion (A): A body in uniform circular motion has a non-zero acceleration.
Reason (R): The direction of its velocity changes continuously even though its speed is constant.

explanation.en: Acceleration is the rate of change of the velocity vector. In uniform circular motion the magnitude is fixed but the direction turns, giving the centripetal acceleration $v^2/r$. R is the reason for A.

options.en: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

stem.en: A ball is projected at 20 m s$^{-1}$ at $45^\circ$ to the horizontal. Its horizontal range is ($g = 10$ m s$^{-2}$):

explanation.en: $R = \dfrac{u^2\sin2\theta}{g} = \dfrac{400\times1}{10} = 40$ m. 20 m is the maximum height for a vertical throw at this speed, $u^2/2g$.

stem.en: Two forces, each of magnitude $F$, act at a point. Their resultant also has magnitude $F$. The angle between the two forces is:

explanation.en: $F^2 = F^2 + F^2 + 2F^2\cos\theta \Rightarrow \cos\theta = -\tfrac12 \Rightarrow \theta = 120^\circ$. Equivalently $2F\cos(\theta/2) = F$ gives $\theta/2 = 60^\circ$; stopping at $60^\circ$ is the usual slip.

stem.en: If $|\vec A + \vec B| = |\vec A - \vec B|$ for two non-zero vectors, the angle between $\vec A$ and $\vec B$ is:

explanation.en: $A^2 + B^2 + 2AB\cos\theta = A^2 + B^2 - 2AB\cos\theta \Rightarrow \cos\theta = 0$, so $\theta = 90^\circ$. Geometrically, the diagonals of the parallelogram are equal only for a rectangle.

stem.en: The component of $\vec A = 2\hat i + 3\hat j$ along the direction of $\hat i + \hat j$ is:

explanation.en: The unit vector is $\hat n = \dfrac{\hat i + \hat j}{\sqrt2}$, so $A_n = \vec A\cdot\hat n = \dfrac{2 + 3}{\sqrt2} = \dfrac{5}{\sqrt2}$. Using $\hat i + \hat j$ without normalising gives 5.

stem.en: A projectile has a time of flight of 4 s and a horizontal range of 80 m on level ground. Its maximum height is ($g = 10$ m s$^{-2}$):

explanation.en: $T = 2u_y/g \Rightarrow u_y = 20$ m s$^{-1}$, so $H = u_y^2/2g = 20$ m (equivalently $gT^2/8 = 160/8$). The range is not needed for $H$; it only gives $u_x = 80/4 = 20$ m s$^{-1}$. 80 m is $gT^2/2$, the drop in 4 s of free fall.

stem.en: The trajectory of a projectile launched from the origin is $y = x - \dfrac{x^2}{20}$ (in metres, with $x$ horizontal and $y$ vertical). Find its horizontal range in metres. (in m)

explanation.en: $y = 0$ at $x = 0$ and $x = 20$ m, so $R = 20$ m. Comparing with $y = x\tan\theta - \dfrac{gx^2}{2u^2\cos^2\theta}$: $\tan\theta = 1$ ($45^\circ$) and $u^2 = 200$, consistent with $R = u^2/g = 20$ m.

stem.en: A river 100 m wide flows at 3 m s$^{-1}$. A boat that moves at 5 m s$^{-1}$ in still water is steered perpendicular to the bank. How far downstream does it land on the opposite bank?

explanation.en: Crossing time $= 100/5 = 20$ s (the river velocity has no component across). Drift $= 3\times20 = 60$ m. 75 m uses the resultant speed 4 m s$^{-1}$ for crossing; 0 m would need the boat to head upstream.

stem.en: In the same river (width 100 m, current 3 m s$^{-1}$, boat speed 5 m s$^{-1}$ in still water), the boat is now steered so that it reaches the point directly opposite its start. Find the crossing time in seconds. (in s)

explanation.en: Head at angle $\theta$ upstream from the normal with $5\sin\theta = 3$, so $\sin\theta = 0.6$ ($\theta \approx 37^\circ$). The component across is $5\cos\theta = 4$ m s$^{-1}$, so $t = 100/4 = 25$ s — longer than the minimum 20 s.

stem.en: Rain falls vertically at 10 m s$^{-1}$. A cyclist rides due east at 10 m s$^{-1}$. To protect himself best, he should hold his umbrella tilted:

explanation.en: $\vec v_{rc} = \vec v_r - \vec v_c = (-10\hat i - 10\hat j)$ m s$^{-1}$: the rain appears to come down at $45^\circ$ from the vertical, from the east (in front). So the umbrella must be tilted forward, toward the east, by $45^\circ$.

options.en: $45^\circ$ from the vertical toward the east
$45^\circ$ from the vertical toward the west
$60^\circ$ from the vertical toward the east

stem.en: Car A moves due north at 30 km h$^{-1}$ and car B moves due east at 40 km h$^{-1}$. The velocity of A relative to B is:

explanation.en: $\vec v_{AB} = 30\hat j - 40\hat i$: 40 km h$^{-1}$ west and 30 km h$^{-1}$ north. Magnitude $= 50$ km h$^{-1}$, direction $\tan^{-1}(30/40) = \tan^{-1}(3/4)$ north of west. "North of east" is $\vec v_A + \vec v_B$.

options.en: $50$ km h$^{-1}$ at $\tan^{-1}(3/4)$ north of west
$50$ km h$^{-1}$ at $\tan^{-1}(3/4)$ north of east

stem.en: A particle moves on a circle of radius 2 m. At an instant when its speed is 4 m s$^{-1}$, the speed is increasing at 3 m s$^{-2}$. Find the magnitude of its total acceleration (in m s$^{-2}$, to two decimal places). (in m s⁻²)

explanation.en: $a_c = v^2/r = 16/2 = 8$ m s$^{-2}$ (toward the centre) and $a_t = 3$ m s$^{-2}$ (along the velocity). $a = \sqrt{8^2 + 3^2} = \sqrt{73} \approx 8.54$ m s$^{-2}$.

stem.en: A particle moves on a circle of radius $R$ with constant speed $v$. The magnitude of its average velocity over half a revolution is:

explanation.en: Displacement $= 2R$; time $= \pi R/v$. So $|\bar{\vec v}| = \dfrac{2R}{\pi R/v} = \dfrac{2v}{\pi}$. The average speed is $v$; the average velocity over a full turn is zero.

stem.en: A particle in uniform circular motion with speed $v$ moves through a quarter of the circle. The magnitude of the change in its velocity is:

explanation.en: $|\Delta\vec v| = |\vec v_2 - \vec v_1| = \sqrt{v^2 + v^2} = \sqrt2\,v$. The speed does not change, but velocity does. $2v$ is the change over half a revolution.

stem.en: A ball is thrown horizontally at 20 m s$^{-1}$ from the top of a 45 m tower. It hits the ground with a velocity of ($g = 10$ m s$^{-2}$):

explanation.en: $v_y = \sqrt{2gh} = \sqrt{900} = 30$ m s$^{-1}$, $v_x = 20$ m s$^{-1}$. $v = \sqrt{400 + 900} = \sqrt{1300} \approx 36.1$ m s$^{-1}$ at $\tan^{-1}(v_y/v_x) = \tan^{-1}(3/2)$ below the horizontal. $\tan^{-1}(2/3)$ inverts the ratio; 50 m s$^{-1}$ adds the components as scalars.

options.en: $50$ m s$^{-1}$ at $45^\circ$ below the horizontal
$36.1$ m s$^{-1}$ at $\tan^{-1}(2/3)$ below the horizontal
$36.1$ m s$^{-1}$ at $\tan^{-1}(3/2)$ below the horizontal

stem.en: The position vector of a particle is $\vec r = 3t\,\hat i + 2t^2\,\hat j$ (SI units). Its speed at $t = 1$ s is:

explanation.en: $\vec v = \dfrac{d\vec r}{dt} = 3\hat i + 4t\,\hat j = 3\hat i + 4\hat j$ at $t = 1$ s, so speed $= 5$ m s$^{-1}$. $\sqrt{13}$ is $|\vec r(1)| = |3\hat i + 2\hat j|$; 7 adds the components. The acceleration is a constant $4\hat j$ m s$^{-2}$.

stem.en:
Statement I: For a projectile on level ground (no air resistance), the speed is least at the highest point.
Statement II: At the highest point, the velocity of the projectile is zero.

explanation.en: $v^2 = u^2\cos^2\theta + v_y^2$ is smallest when $v_y = 0$, at the top — Statement I is true. But the horizontal component $u\cos\theta$ never vanishes (for $\theta \ne 90^\circ$), so the velocity is not zero — Statement II is false.

options.en: Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Statement I is false but Statement II is true

stem.en:
Match each quantity for a projectile (speed $u$, angle $\theta$, level ground) with its expression.
(P) Time of flight  (Q) Maximum height  (R) Horizontal range  (S) Speed at the highest point
(1) $\dfrac{u^2\sin^2\theta}{2g}$  (2) $\dfrac{2u\sin\theta}{g}$  (3) $\dfrac{u^2\sin2\theta}{g}$  (4) $u\cos\theta$

explanation.en: $T = 2u\sin\theta/g$ (P-2), $H = u^2\sin^2\theta/2g$ (Q-1), $R = u^2\sin2\theta/g$ (R-3), and at the top only $u\cos\theta$ remains (S-4). Only (2) has dimensions of time and only (4) of speed, which rules out the other options quickly.

stem.en: A cricketer can throw a ball to a maximum horizontal distance of 100 m on level ground. With the same speed, the greatest height to which he can throw the ball is:

explanation.en: $R_{\max} = u^2/g = 100$ m. Thrown straight up, $H = u^2/2g = 50$ m. 25 m is the maximum height reached during the 45° throw itself ($R_{\max}/4$).

stem.en: Vectors $\vec A$ and $\vec B$ have magnitudes 3 and 5, and $|\vec A + \vec B| = 7$. The angle between $\vec A$ and $\vec B$ is:

explanation.en: $49 = 9 + 25 + 30\cos\theta \Rightarrow \cos\theta = \tfrac12 \Rightarrow \theta = 60^\circ$. Using the cosine rule of the triangle directly ($49 = 9 + 25 - 30\cos\phi$) gives $\phi = 120^\circ$ — that is the angle inside the triangle, not between the vectors.

stem.en: Two vectors of equal magnitude satisfy $|\vec A + \vec B| = \sqrt3\,|\vec A - \vec B|$. The angle between them is:

explanation.en: $2A^2(1 + \cos\theta) = 3\cdot2A^2(1 - \cos\theta) \Rightarrow 1 + \cos\theta = 3 - 3\cos\theta \Rightarrow \cos\theta = \tfrac12$, $\theta = 60^\circ$. Forgetting to square the $\sqrt3$ gives a wrong cosine.

stem.en: Forces of 6 N and 8 N act at a point with an angle of $60^\circ$ between them. Find the magnitude of their resultant in newtons (to two decimal places). (in N)
For a projectile moving under gravity alone, which quantities remain constant throughout the flight?

explanation.en: With only gravity acting, there is no horizontal force, so $v_x$ is constant, and the acceleration is the constant vector $\vec g$. The vertical velocity (and so vertical momentum) changes at rate $g$, so the speed changes too.

stem.en: For a particle in uniform circular motion, which statements are correct?

explanation.en: "Uniform" means constant speed ✓. The velocity's direction changes, so velocity is not constant. The acceleration $v^2/r$ always points to the centre ✓ with constant magnitude ✓ — but its direction rotates, so the acceleration vector itself is not constant either.

options.en: Its acceleration points toward the centre
The magnitude of its acceleration is constant

stem.en: A ball is projected from the bottom of a fixed incline of angle $30^\circ$ with a speed of 20 m s$^{-1}$. Find the maximum range (in m, along the incline) it can achieve up the incline. ($g = 10$ m s$^{-2}$; give two decimal places.) (in m)

explanation.en: Taking axes along and perpendicular to the incline, the range up the incline for launch angle $\beta$ above the incline is $R = \dfrac{2u^2\sin\beta\cos(\alpha+\beta)}{g\cos^2\alpha}$, which is maximum for $\beta = 45^\circ - \alpha/2$, giving $R_{\max} = \dfrac{u^2}{g(1 + \sin\alpha)} = \dfrac{400}{10\times1.5} \approx 26.67$ m. Using the level-ground value $u^2/g = 40$ m ignores the incline.

stem.en: Two projectiles are launched from the same point with the same speed at angles $\theta$ and $(90^\circ - \theta)$ and both land at the same point at distance $R$. The product of their times of flight is:

explanation.en: $T_1T_2 = \dfrac{4u^2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{g^2} = \dfrac{2}{g}\cdot\dfrac{u^2\sin2\theta}{g} = \dfrac{2R}{g}$, independent of $\theta$. Also $T_1/T_2 = \tan\theta$ and $H_1H_2 = R^2/16$.

stem.en: A particle is projected with speed $u$ at angle $\theta$ ($\theta > 45^\circ$) above the horizontal. After what time is its velocity perpendicular to its initial velocity?

explanation.en: $\vec v = u\cos\theta\,\hat i + (u\sin\theta - gt)\hat j$. $\vec v\cdot\vec u = u^2\cos^2\theta + u\sin\theta(u\sin\theta - gt) = u^2 - ugt\sin\theta = 0 \Rightarrow t = \dfrac{u}{g\sin\theta}$. This is before landing only if $\dfrac{u}{g\sin\theta} \le \dfrac{2u\sin\theta}{g}$, i.e. $\theta \ge 45^\circ$. $u\sin\theta/g$ is the time to the top, where $\vec v$ is horizontal, not perpendicular to $\vec u$.

stem.en:
Assertion (A): Two balls are projected at the same instant from different points with different velocities. Seen from one ball, the other moves in a straight line (until either lands).
Reason (R): Both balls have the same acceleration $\vec g$, so their relative acceleration is zero.

explanation.en: $\vec a_{12} = \vec g - \vec g = 0$, so $\vec v_{12}$ is constant and the relative path is a straight line traced at constant speed. R explains A. This is why "will they collide?" problems reduce to checking whether the relative velocity points along the line joining them.

options.en: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

stem.en: A man walking at 3 km h$^{-1}$ finds the rain falling vertically. When he doubles his speed, the rain appears to fall at $45^\circ$ to the vertical. The actual speed of the rain is:

explanation.en: Let $\vec v_r = a\hat i - b\hat j$. At 3 km h$^{-1}$: $\vec v_r - 3\hat i$ is vertical $\Rightarrow a = 3$. At 6 km h$^{-1}$: $\vec v_r - 6\hat i = -3\hat i - b\hat j$ at $45^\circ \Rightarrow b = 3$. Actual speed $= \sqrt{9 + 9} = 3\sqrt2$ km h$^{-1}$, at $45^\circ$ to the vertical. Assuming the rain is truly vertical leads to 3 km h$^{-1}$.

stem.en: A river 100 m wide flows at 4 m s$^{-1}$. A boat can move at only 2 m s$^{-1}$ relative to the water. Find the minimum possible downstream drift (in m) as the boat crosses the river (to one decimal place). (in m)

explanation.en: The resultant $\vec v = \vec v_{river} + \vec v_{boat}$ has its tip on a circle of radius 2 centred 4 units downstream. The steepest resultant is tangent to that circle: $\sin\alpha = 2/4$, $\alpha = 30^\circ$ with the bank (the boat is headed perpendicular to this resultant, at $120^\circ$ to the current). Drift $= \dfrac{100}{\tan30^\circ} = 100\sqrt3 \approx 173.2$ m. Heading straight across would give $4\times(100/2) = 200$ m.

stem.en: A particle starts from rest and moves on a circle of radius 1 m with speed $v = 2t$ (m s$^{-1}$). At what time (in s, to two decimal places) does its total acceleration make an angle of $45^\circ$ with its velocity? (in s)

explanation.en: $a_t = dv/dt = 2$ m s$^{-2}$ and $a_c = v^2/r = 4t^2$. The angle with the velocity is $45^\circ$ when $a_c = a_t$: $4t^2 = 2 \Rightarrow t = 1/\sqrt2 \approx 0.71$ s.

stem.en: A ball is projected at $20\sqrt2$ m s$^{-1}$ at $45^\circ$ above the horizontal on level ground ($g = 10$ m s$^{-2}$). Which statements are correct?

options.en: Its time of flight is $2\sqrt2$ s
Its speed at $t = 1$ s is $10\sqrt5$ m s$^{-1}$

stem.en: A ball is thrown from the top of a 20 m high tower at 20 m s$^{-1}$ at $30^\circ$ above the horizontal. How far from the foot of the tower does it land? ($g = 10$ m s$^{-2}$)

explanation.en: $u_y = 10$ m s$^{-1}$, $u_x = 10\sqrt3 \approx 17.32$ m s$^{-1}$. $-20 = 10t - 5t^2 \Rightarrow t^2 - 2t - 4 = 0 \Rightarrow t = 1 + \sqrt5 \approx 3.24$ s. $x = 17.32\times3.24 \approx 56.0$ m. 34.6 m is the level-ground range; 40 m treats the throw as horizontal.

stem.en: The position of a particle is $\vec r = 2t\,\hat i + (t^2 - 4t)\,\hat j$ (SI units). Which statements are correct?

explanation.en: $\vec v = 2\hat i + (2t - 4)\hat j$ — at $t = 2$ s it is $2\hat i$ ✓, and that is also when the speed $\sqrt{4 + (2t-4)^2}$ is least ✓. $\vec a = 2\hat j$ ✓. With $x = 2t$: $y = \dfrac{x^2}{4} - 2x$, a parabola, so C is false (constant acceleration not parallel to velocity gives a parabola).

options.en: At $t = 2$ s its velocity is directed along $+\hat i$
Its acceleration is a constant $2\hat j$ m s$^{-2}$
Its path is a straight line
Its speed is minimum at t = 2 s
